title: Postgres Indexing: When to Pick BRIN Over B-Tree for Big Tables
excerpt: B-Trees offer O(log N) point lookups but eat gigabytes of RAM. Here is when Block Range Indexes (BRIN) slash index sizes by 99% with identical scan speed.
content:
# Postgres Indexing: When to Pick BRIN Over B-Tree for Big Tables

When scaling PostgreSQL tables past 100 million rows, standard B-Tree indexes quickly become a bottleneck. A B-Tree on a `created_at` or auto-incrementing ID column often consumes more storage than the raw table data itself, pushing active working sets out of `shared_buffers`.

## Anatomy of a B-Tree vs BRIN

A **B-Tree** maintains a balanced tree of every single heap tuple pointer (CTID):
- Storage overhead: ~32 bytes per index entry.
- Point lookup: 3-4 random page reads.
- Size on 200M rows: ~8-12 GB.

A **BRIN (Block Range Index)** divides table heap pages into ranges (default 128 pages = 1MB) and records only the minimum and maximum values for each range:

```sql
-- Create a standard B-Tree on timestamp
CREATE INDEX idx_logs_timestamp_btree ON audit_logs (created_at);
-- Size: 9.4 GB on 150M rows

-- Create a BRIN index on timestamp
CREATE INDEX idx_logs_timestamp_brin ON audit_logs 
USING BRIN (created_at) WITH (pages_per_range = 64);
-- Size: 18 MB on 150M rows (99.8% smaller!)
```

## When BRIN Works

BRIN relies on physical correlation between disk block placement and column values. Check correlation with:

```sql
SELECT attname, correlation 
FROM pg_stats 
WHERE tablename = 'audit_logs' AND attname = 'created_at';
```

If correlation is close to `1.0` (such as append-only time-series data or sequential UUIDv7/SERIAL columns), Postgres skips non-matching ranges entirely during bitmap index scans.

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT count(*)
FROM audit_logs
WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-09-02';
```

```text
Bitmap Heap Scan on audit_logs (cost=21.40..4931.20 rows=82400 width=8)
  Recheck Cond: ((created_at >= '2026-09-01'::timestamp) AND (created_at < '2026-09-02'::timestamp))
  ->  Bitmap Index Scan on idx_logs_timestamp_brin (cost=0.00..20.80 rows=82400 width=0)
```

## Takeaways

- Use **B-Tree** for high-cardinality point lookups (`WHERE api_key = ?`), unique constraints, and columns with random distributions.
- Use **BRIN** for append-only logs, event streams, and time-partitioned tables where values are ordered by ingestion.

title: Optimizing Docker Multi-Stage Builds: Layer Cache Ordering & BuildKit Mounts
excerpt: Slash CI build times from 8 minutes to 25 seconds by isolating lockfiles, leveraging BuildKit cache mounts, and building minimal scratch images.
content:
# Optimizing Docker Multi-Stage Builds: Layer Cache Ordering & BuildKit Mounts

Most Docker container images suffer from unnecessary bloat and thrash CI caches on every commit. By understanding BuildKit's directed acyclic graph (DAG) evaluator, you can write production container builds that run in seconds.

## 1. Split Manifest Copying from Source Copying

Docker evaluates each instruction against the checksum of the build context and image layer. Copying application source before installing package dependencies invalidates the dependency cache on every single code edit.

```dockerfile
# SYNTAX=docker/dockerfile:1.4
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# Step 1: Copy only package manifests
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./

# Step 2: Leverage BuildKit cache mount for npm cache
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --prefer-offline --no-audit

# Step 3: Copy rest of application code ONLY after deps are cached
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
```

## 2. Minimal Production Runtime Image

Never ship compilers, test suites, or package managers to production containers. Use a multi-stage target:

```dockerfile
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12:nonroot AS runner
WORKDIR /app

# Copy only the compiled artifacts and production dependencies
COPY --from=builder --chown=nonroot:nonroot /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=builder --chown=nonroot:nonroot /app/node_modules ./node_modules

USER nonroot
EXPOSE 3000
ENV NODE_ENV=production
CMD ["dist/server.js"]
```

## Benchmark Comparison

| Metric | Naive Dockerfile | Multi-Stage + BuildKit |
|---|---|---|
| Image Size | 1.14 GB | 64 MB |
| Cold Build (CI) | 6m 45s | 1m 12s |
| Incremental (Code edit) | 4m 10s | 9s |
| CVE Vulnerabilities | 42 | 0 |

title: Git Storage Model Demystified: Blobs, Trees, Commits, and Packfiles
excerpt: Underneath the CLI, Git is an elegant content-addressable key-value object store. Here is how SHA-1 hashes, directory trees, and pack delta compression store code.
content:
# Git Storage Model Demystified: Blobs, Trees, Commits, and Packfiles

Git is not a diff-tracking VCS; it is a content-addressable filesystem. The `.git/objects` folder stores all project history across four primary primitive types: `blob`, `tree`, `commit`, and `tag`.

## 1. Blobs (Binary Large Objects)

A blob stores raw file content without filenames, permissions, or timestamps. The object key is computed as the SHA-1 or SHA-256 hash of `blob <byte_count>\0<content>`:

```bash
$ echo -n "hello devlog" | git hash-object --stdin -w
# Output: d3b95a8e0cb2049d56485e9a4f4efbc699b823e4

$ file .git/objects/d3/b95a8e0cb2049d56485e9a4f4efbc699b823e4
# Output: zlib compressed data
```

## 2. Trees (Directories)

A `tree` object models directories. It maps filenames and POSIX permissions (`100644` for regular file, `040000` for subtree) to the hashes of blobs or child trees:

```text
100644 blob d3b95a8e0cb2...    README.md
100755 blob a9f182c401e2...    deploy.sh
040000 tree e69de29bb2d1...    src
```

## 3. Commits

A `commit` object points to a root `tree` object, one or more parent commit hashes, author/committer identities, and a commit message:

```text
tree 82fa9168b4ef2134a9b
parent 3c72b110998a4d193ef
author Linus <author@kernel.org> 1759000000 +0000
committer Linus <author@kernel.org> 1759000000 +0000

Initial architecture rewrite
```

## Packfiles and Sliding-Window Delta Compression

If Git stored each version as an independent compressed loose object, repositories would balloon exponentially. Periodically (`git gc`), Git bundles loose objects into `.pack` files using sliding-window byte delta compression:

```bash
$ git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/pack-*.idx | sort -k3nr | head -n 5
```

In a packfile, Git stores the newest file in full, and older revisions as backwards diffs, optimizing checkout speed for HEAD.

title: SQLite WAL Mode: High Concurrency for Embedded Workloads
excerpt: Turn off default rollback journals and unleash concurrent multi-reader single-writer throughput with SQLite Write-Ahead Logging.
content:
# SQLite WAL Mode: High Concurrency for Embedded Workloads

By default, SQLite uses a rollback journal for ACID transactions. When a write transaction begins, SQLite acquires an exclusive file lock, completely freezing all concurrent readers. Enabling WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) changes this game.

## Enabling WAL Mode

```sql
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;
PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;
```

Executing `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;` creates two auxiliary files alongside `database.db`:
1. `database.db-wal` (The actual append-only log)
2. `database.db-shm` (Shared-memory index mapping block offsets)

## How Concurrent Readers and Writers Intersect

In WAL mode:
- **Writers** append new transaction pages to the end of the `-wal` file without modifying the main database file.
- **Readers** determine their snapshot transaction point and read updated pages from `-wal` (indexed by `-shm`) or older unmodified pages from `database.db`.
- **Zero Blocking:** Readers never block writers. Writers never block readers.

## The Checkpoint Process

When the WAL file hits a size threshold (default 1,000 pages), SQLite runs a checkpoint operation copying WAL pages back to the database file:

```sql
PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE);
```

Setting `synchronous = NORMAL` in WAL mode still guarantees durability across OS crashes because transaction frames are checksummed, while eliminating fsync stalls on every commit.

title: Raft Consensus: Leader Election, Log Replication, & Split Brains
excerpt: How distributed nodes agree on a single source of truth across network partitions using randomized heartbeats and majority quorums.
content:
# Raft Consensus: Leader Election, Log Replication, & Split Brains

Unlike Paxos, which is notoriously difficult to comprehend and implement, Raft decomposes consensus into three independent sub-problems: Leader Election, Log Replication, and Safety.

## The Three Node States

At any instant, a Raft cluster node is in one of three states:
1. **Follower:** Responds to RPCs from candidates and leaders. If election timeout expires without heartbeats, transitions to Candidate.
2. **Candidate:** Requests votes from peers for a new term.
3. **Leader:** Handles all client requests, replicates log entries, and sends periodic heartbeat AppendEntries RPCs.

## Preventing Split Votes with Randomized Timeouts

If two followers time out at the identical millisecond, both trigger elections and split the votes evenly. Raft elegantly avoids this through randomized election timeouts (e.g., 150ms – 300ms):

```text
Node A Timeout: 172ms ---> Starts election first, claims quorum!
Node B Timeout: 285ms ---> Resets timer upon receiving Node A's vote request
Node C Timeout: 240ms ---> Votes for Node A
```

## Log Replication and Quorum

A cluster of $2F + 1$ nodes tolerates $F$ simultaneous node failures:

```text
Client write: SET user:1 = "elena"
      │
      ▼
[ Leader ] ──── AppendEntries RPC ────► [ Follower 1 ] (ACK)
    │                                        │
    └───────── AppendEntries RPC ────► [ Follower 2 ] (Timeout / Down)

Majority achieved: 2 of 3 nodes acknowledged.
Leader commits entry to state machine and returns success to client.
```

## Log Matching Safety Invariant

If two logs contain an entry with the same index and term:
- They store the same command.
- All entries in previous indexes are identical.

During recovery, the leader forces followers to duplicate its own log by finding the latest consensus point and overwriting conflicting follower entries.

title: Kafka Partitions at Scale: Consumer Group Rebalancing & Zero-Copy I/O
excerpt: Under the hood of Apache Kafka: OS page cache utilization, sendfile() DMA zero-copy transfers, and avoiding rebalance storms.
content:
# Kafka Partitions at Scale: Consumer Group Rebalancing & Zero-Copy I/O

Apache Kafka routinely delivers millions of messages per second on modest hardware. Its secret lies not in custom memory architectures, but in deep synergy with the Linux virtual memory and page cache.

## The Zero-Copy sendfile() Path

Traditional application servers transfer files to network sockets through four context switches and three buffer copies:
1. Disk $\to$ OS Page Cache (Kernel)
2. Page Cache $\to$ Application User Buffer (Userspace copy)
3. Application User Buffer $\to$ Socket Buffer (Kernel copy)
4. Socket Buffer $\to$ NIC Buffer (DMA)

Kafka eliminates steps 2 and 3 using the `sendfile(2)` system call:

```c
#include <sys/sendfile.h>

// Direct kernel-space transfer from file descriptor to network socket
sendfile(socket_fd, file_fd, &offset, count);
```

Bytes stream directly from OS page cache into the Network Interface Card (NIC) via Direct Memory Access (DMA), consuming zero CPU cycles for copying.

## Avoiding Consumer Group Rebalance Storms

When a consumer misses a heartbeat or is stuck processing a batch longer than `max.poll.interval.ms`, the Group Coordinator evicts it and halts processing across all group members for a rebalance.

### Mitigation Checklist
- Use **Cooperative Sticky Assignor** (`CooperativeStickyAssignor`) to perform incremental rebalances without stopping the world.
- Tune `max.poll.records` down to ensure batches finish well within `max.poll.interval.ms`.
- Partition keys must be evenly distributed to prevent single-partition consumer starvation.

title: HTTP/3 and QUIC: Eradicating TCP Head-of-Line Blocking
excerpt: HTTP/2 multiplexed streams over a single TCP pipe, introducing transport-level HOL blocking on packet drop. Here is how QUIC over UDP fixes it.
content:
# HTTP/3 and QUIC: Eradicating TCP Head-of-Line Blocking

HTTP/2 revolutionized web delivery by multiplexing dozens of concurrent request streams over a single TCP connection, eliminating browser domain sharding. However, on lossy mobile networks (cellular, flaky Wi-Fi), HTTP/2 often performed **worse** than multiple HTTP/1.1 connections.

## The TCP Head-of-Line (HOL) Flaw

TCP guarantees byte-stream delivery in strict monotonic order:

```text
Stream A: Packet 1 [OK]
Stream B: Packet 2 [DROPPED in transit]
Stream A: Packet 3 [Arrived at client kernel]

TCP Kernel Stack: Packet 3 is held in receive buffer until Packet 2 
is retransmitted. Stream A is completely blocked by Stream B's loss!
```

A single dropped packet stalls **all** active streams in HTTP/2.

## Enter QUIC: Streams at the Transport Layer

HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC, running over UDP. QUIC natively recognizes independent stream IDs in its packet headers:

```text
QUIC Packet 1 (Stream 1) -> Delivered
QUIC Packet 2 (Stream 2) -> Dropped
QUIC Packet 3 (Stream 1) -> Delivered and immediately dispatched to app!
```

Stream 1 experiences zero latency delay while Stream 2 handles retransmission.

## 0-RTT Connection Resumption

QUIC folds TLS 1.3 cryptographic handshakes directly into the transport handshake, allowing clients to send application HTTP requests in their very first packet to previously visited servers.

title: Go's Garbage Collector: Tri-Color Mark-and-Sweep & Pacing
excerpt: How the Go runtime achieves sub-millisecond Stop-The-World (STW) pauses with concurrent tri-color marking and hybrid write barriers.
content:
# Go's Garbage Collector: Tri-Color Mark-and-Sweep & Pacing

Unlike the JVM or V8, which rely on complex generational hypotheses with young and old generations, Go uses a non-generational, concurrent tri-color mark-and-sweep collector optimized for low latency.

## The Tri-Color Abstraction

During garbage collection, all heap objects are classified into three sets:
- **White:** Unreached objects (candidates for sweeping).
- **Grey:** Reached objects whose referenced children have not yet been scanned.
- **Black:** Reached objects whose pointers have all been scanned.

```text
Initial State: All objects are White.
1. Roots (goroutine stacks, global vars) marked Grey.
2. Concurrent Worker picks Grey object, scans its pointers, marks it Black.
3. Repeat until Grey set is empty.
4. All remaining White objects are swept.
```

## The Hybrid Write Barrier

Because marking runs concurrently while application goroutines are running, an active goroutine could hide an allocated white object behind a black object, leading to premature deallocation.

Go prevents this using a **Hybrid Write Barrier**:
- Any pointer overwritten on the heap is shaded grey.
- Any object allocated during an active GC phase is marked black immediately.

```go
// Runtime pseudo-code for write barrier
func writePointer(slot *uintptr, newObj uintptr) {
    if gcphase == _GCmark {
        shade(*slot) // Shade existing pointer
    }
    *slot = newObj
}
```

## GC Pacing & GOGC Tuning

The Go scheduler reserves 25% of CPU cores for background GC marking workers, balancing application throughput with sub-millisecond STW pause times.
